title: The Master Maid
place: A giant’s mountain hall and a northern kingdom
sourceTitle: Popular Tales from the Norse, “The Mastermaid”
sourceAuthor: Peter Christen Asbjørnsen and Jørgen Moe; translated by George Webbe Dasent
note: A substantially condensed reading copy of Dasent’s public-domain English translation in the cited 1903 edition. It retains the prince’s service, the Master Maid’s three counsels, their magical flight, the apple of forgetfulness, and recognition at the wedding. The long comic sequence of failed suitors at her golden hut is omitted, and repeated dialogue is shortened; spelling and punctuation are lightly modernized. The illustrations are newly generated because the cited edition supplies no suitable story plates.

rights.basis: The cited 1903 David Douglas edition was published before 1931 and is public domain in the United States.

artLabel: At the giant’s mountain hall, the prince first glimpses the wise Master Maid.
scenes: A king’s youngest son sailed away to seek his fortune. After a storm carried him far from home, he came to a strange shore and entered a giant’s service. The giant forbade him to enter four rooms, then left him to clean a stable that could never be emptied by ordinary work.

The prince opened the forbidden rooms. In three, magical kettles turned locks of his hair copper, silver, and gold. In the fourth sat a lovely, clever princess called the Master Maid. She told him to turn the pitchfork upside down and work with its handle. At once the stable cleaned itself.

Next the giant ordered him to fetch a fire-breathing horse. The Master Maid showed him a bit that would tame it. On the third day the giant demanded his fire-tax from inside a blazing rock; following her counsel, the prince asked for only as much treasure as he could carry. Each task was safely done.

The giant guessed who had helped him and ordered the Master Maid to kill and boil the prince. Instead she put three drops of his blood on a stool to answer the giant’s calls, packed a chest with gold, and fled with the prince across the sea.

When the giant discovered the trick, he pursued them. He drained the sea with the help of his stream-sucker, but the Master Maid had the prince cast a lump of salt behind them. It rose into a mountain. When the giant bored through, a drop from her flask restored the sea, and the fugitives reached land.

Near his father’s palace, the prince insisted on fetching horses for her. The Master Maid warned him neither to greet anyone nor taste food. But a bride’s sister rolled an apple across the yard. He bit it and instantly forgot the Master Maid, leaving her alone by the shore.

The Master Maid made a humble hut shine with gold and waited. When the prince was to marry another, she entered the wedding feast. Her golden cock and hen enacted their adventures and reproached the forgetful prince before the whole company.

Memory returned. The prince knew the Master Maid who had saved his life again and again. He chose her as his true bride, and the false wedding became their own. So cleverness and constancy won at last.

pageArt.alt: The Master Maid and prince race beside a fjord while a magical forest blocks the pursuing giant.
At the wedding feast the prince remembers the Master Maid and joyfully takes her hand.
